steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening at dusk, Martin climbed the 112 steps.

He had counted them so many times that the number had lost its meaning, become something closer to a heartbeat than a thought. One hundred and twelve. His knees ached on cold nights. He climbed anyway.

The lighthouse sat on a shelf of black rock off the Maine coast, connected to the mainland by a causeway that flooded at high tide. For eight months of the year, Martin was essentially alone. He had a radio, a library of paperback novels with soft, curved spines, and a cat named Ptolemy who had shown up one spring in a supply crate and never left.

People assumed the job was lonely. Martin never bothered to correct them.

He had been a loud man once — a husband, a father, a man who filled rooms. Then the rooms had emptied, one by one, through the ordinary catastrophes of a life lived long enough. He had applied for the posting on a Tuesday afternoon, sitting at a kitchen table that was too large for one person, looking at a coffee cup that was just his.

The Coast Guard had modernized the light years ago. It ran itself, technically. Martin's duties were maintenance, record-keeping, weather observation. What he actually did was watch.

He watched the water change colors — green to grey to black to a particular shade of blue that existed nowhere else on earth, that he had never seen described in any book, that he kept trying to name and couldn't. He watched storms build on the horizon like slow arguments. He watched tankers and fishing boats pass in the dark, their lights moving with a patience that comforted him.

And occasionally, not often, he guided someone home.

A kayaker caught in a sudden squall. A sailboat that had lost its GPS and was running frightened in the dark. Once, memorably, a man in a small motorboat who had simply gone out without telling anyone where, and who wept when the beam found him.

Martin never spoke of these moments as heroic. He had simply been present. He had kept the light.

On a Thursday in November, a letter arrived with the supply boat. The Coast Guard was automating his position fully. They thanked him for his service. They offered him a modest pension. They gave him sixty days.

Martin read the letter twice, then set it on the table and climbed the 112 steps.

From the top, he could see the mainland — a scattered necklace of lights along the shore. He could see the dark water between. He stood there while Ptolemy wound between his ankles and the great lamp turned slowly behind him, throwing its arm of light across the sea.

He thought about the kayaker. The weeping man. The blue that had no name.

He thought that some things needed a person behind them. Not because the light itself wasn't enough. But because some nights what the dark needed wasn't just a signal.

It needed to know that someone, somewhere, was watching. Was still there. Was keeping it in mind.

He went downstairs and wrote back to the Coast Guard.

He asked if he could stay another season. Just one more.

He was still waiting for their answer when the first winter storm came in, and he climbed the stairs, and turned the light on early, just in case.
